💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday.
  • The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.
  • The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump conducts a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The penny is officially history under a bill President Donald Trump signed into law Friday that codifies the end of production of the one-cent piece.

The copper-plated coin is mostly composed of zinc and costs far more to produce than it's worth, prompting members of Congress at least since 1989 to consider killing it as an easy cost-saving measure for the federal government.

“Washington has a spending problem, and it shows up in places big and small,” the bill's sponsor, Rep. Lisa McClain, R-Mich., said Friday in a statement released by the office of House Financial Services Chairman French Hill, R-Ark. “If the federal government is spending nearly four cents to make a penny worth one cent, something is broken.”.

Hill mentioned in the statement that the bill also provides "clear legislative guidance for retailers, financial institutions, and consumers," referring to the measure's requirements that cash transactions not settled with exact change will be rounded to the nearest nickel.

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies a year ago under an executive order. Pennies already in circulation will still be legal tender, and the Mint may still issue special collectors editions. The legislation, named the Common Cents Act, also sets composition specifications for nickels.

Like a well-traveled coin, the bill itself took a winding road to the White House. The House originally passed a similar bill in July and the Senate passed its version by unanimous consent on Aug. 7.

It has been revealed that but the Senate added a section that would require the Treasury secretary to notify Congress before discontinuing other coins. That sent the bill back to the House with a Senate number.

As the sponsor of the original measure, McClain insisted that the legislation have a House bill number. So, she reintroduced the revised Senate version, and the House voted on it on Sept. 14. The Senate passed it once again by unanimous consent on Sept. 28, sending it to the president's desk.

Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said the bill “modernizes our currency system and most importantly gives families and businesses clear rules for everyday cash transactions.”.

#122452. America’s Hidden AI Advantage

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2258 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

America’s Hidden AI Advantage

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.
  • Sources indicate that in the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy.
  • This narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.

The United States—Not China—Dominates Diffusion.

Sources indicate that in the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy. Even if the United States has a small lead in frontier AI models, the consensus is that China is better at applying the technology. As Kevin Rudd, former prime minister of Australia and a prominent observer of Chinese politics, declared at a conference in October, China is “miles ahead” in spreading AI “into the real economy.” This fits a familiar narrative about the technological rivalry between the two great powers: the United States innovates while China turns those innovations into practical applications at scale.

This narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI. But it doesn’t match reality. After the Chinese startup DeepSeek shocked the world in early 2025 with the announcement of an open-source large language model that rivaled the capabilities of frontier models made by American companies, the international media published breathless reports on how DeepSeek’s model had rapidly spread across state-owned enterprises, hospitals, and provincial and local governments. Months later, however, analysts determined that this adoption was shallow, narrow, and slow; the technology was being used on clunky “all-in-one machines” embedded on isolated hardware units within these institutions, rather than integrated more broadly into the software services they were using. Then, in January 2026, outside observers marveled at OpenClaw, a newly introduced open-source AI agent, as a sign of China’s diffusion advantage. Now, the excitement about these open-source agents has dissipated as security vulnerabilities and inefficiency have limited their uptake.

In a recent development, it is the United States, not China, that has a decisive lead in AI diffusion. This is because the United States has comparative advantages in both its overall level of economic development and the nature of its growth model. China’s underdeveloped software market, weak technology transfer mechanisms, and centralized economic system make AI diffusion much more challenging. All told, the United States’ advantage in diffusing the technology through the economy is likely to persist for the foreseeable future.

Despite its reputation as a pioneer of digital technology such as cashless payments and messaging apps, China’s overall digitization levels—the extent to which software and other digital tools have penetrated various sectors of the economy—are far lower than those in the United States. American firms are on average more than twice as likely as their Chinese competitors to adopt cloud computing services. And the U.S. enterprise software market, which includes services to manage customer relationships and provide business intelligence, is approximately ten times larger than China’s. According to the 2022 Global Cloud Ecosystem Index, which ranked 76 countries on their access to and usage of cloud services, China sat in the bottom half; the United States, by contrast, ranked 17th, not far behind the top performers, in part because of its dominance of “software as a service” products in which businesses can gain access to enterprise software without needing to install and maintain the programs themselves.

It has been revealed that china’s relatively low penetration of digital services is a barrier to diffusing AI. When small Chinese hospitals tried to adopt DeepSeek, for instance, they lacked information systems that could collect and manage the data necessary to take full advantage of AI models. In these hospitals, which include many small health facilities in rural areas, patient data is still recorded on paper; where digital records do exist, they are often incomplete or vary from hospital to hospital. By contrast, 95 percent of U.S. doctors maintain electronic health record systems in their offices. As a result, U.S. hospitals have more smoothly integrated AI into electronic health records to recommend treatments, predict health risks, and simplify billing.

Industry observers note that china’s underdeveloped cloud and enterprise software ecosystem also explains why the OpenClaw hype did not translate to sustainable diffusion. Open-source tools like OpenClaw appeal to hobbyists and individual developers who are keen to experiment and are less sensitive to security concerns. But small businesses have been slow to adopt such tools because they prefer reliable, standardized solutions that are easy to implement and update. Small businesses are more likely to rely on cloud-based tools and enterprise software to implement AI upgrades than to try to experiment on their own—two channels that are less robust in China than in the United States.

The United States also has an advantage over China because of linkages within the science and technology ecosystem that help disseminate advances. Collaboration between universities and businesses is critical to diffusing AI breakthroughs across the entire economy because these connections bring together innovators who can develop new AI products and implementers who can effectively commercialize them.

In this dimension, the United States is far ahead of China. Americans have long led the world in the publication of articles about AI co-authored by at least one researcher from academia and one researcher from industry. Between 2015 and 2019, U.S. researchers published more than twice as many such articles as their Chinese counterparts. The gap extends beyond AI: across the life sciences and natural sciences, the share of publications in the United States that involved both university and industry researchers was also more than double the comparable rate in China. Beijing recognizes this gap: China’s official state news agency ranked weak technical exchanges between industry and academia as one of the five crucial shortcomings of the country’s AI ecosystem.

Although Chinese policymakers are aware of this challenge and have promoted policies to try to spur collaboration between universities and businesses, especially in AI, it will be difficult to cultivate the requisite trust needed for these two sectors to work together. China’s weak intellectual property protections, for example, discourage universities from pursuing partnerships with industry actors because they fear losing ownership of their inventions. The United States, by contrast, has a tradition of university-industry collaboration. The 1980 Bayh-Dole Act, which provides incentives and patent protections that encourage universities to commercialize inventions and license them to the private sector, kick-started decades of collaboration. Without a similar connective tissue to link academic institutions and businesses, Chinese universities are not as equipped to form profitable partnerships with companies. Chinese technical and engineering education is also disconnected from commercial enterprises, meaning that schools do not teach students the specific skills that companies need in their workforces.

Weak technology transfer mechanisms also undermine one of China’s main strengths in AI diffusion: its massive talent base. Analysis by the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation demonstrated that in 2022, China awarded around 50,000 doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering, and math, compared with only about 34,000 in the United States. Although the sheer quantity of Chinese computer science graduates may eventually help the country adopt AI advances at scale, the quality of that education determines how swiftly or effectively education can encourage AI diffusion. If training is divorced from practical applications, graduates will struggle to adapt cutting-edge advances from industry labs into the sectors in which they work. Consider one commonly used standard to measure the baseline quality of AI education: whether a university employs at least one researcher who has published at least one paper at a leading AI conference. According to data from 2023–24, only 38 universities in China met this standard; the United States accounted for 150.

China’s centrally planned approach to AI development is also counterproductive when it comes to diffusion. In 2025, China developed an “AI Plus” action blueprint that outlines targets for AI adoption over the next decade and released guidelines for government agencies and local officials on how to put the plan into effect across the country. For many observers, the mere existence of a plan showed that the highest levels of Chinese leadership were committed to spreading AI widely and that China was better positioned to win the AI race than the United States, which lacks any kind of similar diffusion blueprint. Rudd’s claims about China’s edge in AI adoption, for instance, cite Beijing’s ambitious policies and targets for AI diffusion as supporting evidence.

Recent findings suggest that but centralized approaches such as China’s often impede technology diffusion, especially when the state tries to intervene in domains in which the development trajectory is uncertain. One of the planks of China’s AI Plus strategy identifies “global cooperation” as a priority sector for AI adoption. If local governments were to implement the plan as outlined, it would shift resources from areas in which diffusion has been proven to be effective, such as health care, to the undefined space of “global cooperation.” More broadly, Beijing’s favoritism toward state-owned enterprises and its preference for picking national champions often prop up inefficient technologies that would have been weeded out by market-based competition. Other businesses are unlikely to adopt inefficient technologies, making nonmarket forms of AI development less likely to diffuse widely.

In a recent development, counterintuitively, the lack of a clear U.S. policy on AI diffusion is a boon, not a hindrance, to the United States’ attempt to diffuse the technology across the economy. At the height of U.S.-Japanese competition in the 1980s, for instance, when the two countries were racing to train software engineers who could spread computer technology, Japan’s Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture, as it was then known, exercised centralized control over universities. But emerging trends in computer science developed faster than the government could adapt. By concentrating state funds on centers of excellence and imposing one-size-fits-all rules on the computing curriculum, Japan could not match the adaptability of American universities, and the United States surged ahead. Cross-national studies have shown that decentralized science and technology systems are correlated with faster diffusion of fresh innovations.

Another historical case with parallels to China, the Soviet Union, further suggests how centralization is antithetical to diffusion. In the twentieth century, the Soviet Union boasted many intends for technology development. Yet its top-down approach, which focused on large-scale engineering projects, undercut market-based instruments that encourage technology diffusion through competition. As a result, although the Soviet Union pioneered upcoming technologies in many areas, including the casting of steel, it fell behind the United States in adopting general-purpose technologies such as computers. A prescient U.S. intelligence report published in 1969 deemed the Soviet Union’s mechanisms for technology diffusion as “much more balky” than those of the United States because of the absence of competitive pressures as well as limited linkages between the R & D system and the broader economy.

According to recent reports, the myth of China’s lead in AI diffusion persists despite clear data showing U.S. advantages. In part, this may be because China’s innovation system has facilitated the widespread adoption of certain visible technologies. In less than 20 years, China has built more than 30,000 miles of high-speed rail, for example, blanketing the country with ultra-fast trains that now reach even the most remote provinces.

In a recent development, but infrastructure presents a very different challenge than AI does. The centralized pressure that officials can use to effectively develop large-scale infrastructure projects is much less effective for general-purpose technologies like AI because it is infeasible to mandate that all small- and medium-size firms, spread across every sector of the economy, adopt artificial intelligence. Those companies would do so only if it made sense from a business perspective, and few have the digital foundations or savvy employees able to harness AI in a way that would help them grow. Moreover, the United States has outbuilt China in the infrastructure most essential to AI development, data centers, in which it retains a ten-to-one edge. In fact, in some cases, the data centers that China has built remain idle because of weak AI demand.

According to recent reports, the misperception that China leads AI diffusion may continue unabated because analysis of the country’s technology ecosystem is overly focused on frontier firms such as ByteDance and DeepSeek and first-tier cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai. Yet AI diffusion ultimately rests on whether adoption occurs in medium size companies, small towns, and inland provinces, where it has been extremely limited. Because these settings rarely feature in outside media coverage, analysis of China’s AI diffusion landscape underestimates the difficulty of translating cutting-edge advances from frontier labs and universities in Hangzhou or Shenzhen to, say, a small firm in a county seat in northwestern Qinghai Province.

In a recent development, perhaps the simplest explanation is that such a myth is useful, even if ultimately untrue. In some ways, the United States is trumpeting Beijing’s AI diffusion in the way that Chinese “tiger parents” try to motivate their children to work harder by raising the success of “that other family’s kid.” “Look at how well that other family’s kid performed at the piano recital,” they might say, without listening closely to ensure that the notes were exactly right. In great-power rivalry, too, there is a natural tendency to overhype the other side’s capabilities, in part to spur more effort at home.

Recent findings suggest that but such a “useful” myth can backfire if it pushes the United States to overlook its own advantages or even to mimic China’s more top-down approach to AI development. By any measure, the United States maintains a comfortable lead in AI diffusion, and China, despite its impressive successes, has serious challenges. Although the narrative of Chinese dominance endures, for now all signs point to a U.S. lead that will remain strong.

Retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack breaks down what sits inside America’s law enforcement computers, how hackers get in and how to protect your data.

A retired FBI supervisory special agent warned Saturday that a cyber intrusion into the bureau's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) could endanger police officers during traffic stops if hackers altered records inside the database.

Jason Pack, a former FBI supervisory special agent who worked in cybercrime and public information, told Fox News Digital that the bureau's incident response team must promptly determine whether data was manipulated inside the system, which feeds criminal records to patrol cars nationwide.

"What they worry about is if any of this data has changed, then it might affect officers' safety on the side of the road," Pack said, noting there is no indication yet that any records were altered or that the system is experiencing an outage.

FBI PROBES SECOND CYBERATTACK IN MONTHS AS HACKERS BREACH KEY CRIME DATABASE, SOURCES SAY.

Recent findings suggest that hackers have targeted the FBI for the second time in recent months. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters, File).

In a recent development, three sources familiar with the matter told Fox News that hackers breached the NCIC, marking the second cyberattack against the bureau in months. The FBI is investigating how the intruders gained entry and whether any information was compromised.

In an interview with Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany on Saturday morning, President Donald Trump mentioned he had "just heard" about the intrusion, adding, "I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that.".

Pack described the NCIC as "America's computer for law enforcement," explaining that roughly 56 state terminals feed data out to hundreds of thousands of patrol car computers, so officers can check warrants, criminal histories, missing children, gang members and suspected terrorists.

FBI NOTES SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED.

While the database does not hold classified intelligence or sensitive FBI investigative case files, Pack noted it stores personally identifiable information, including names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers.

Investigators will examine IP logs and metadata to determine whether attackers exploited a compromised password among the system's more than 100,000 owners, breached a state terminal or infiltrated through a third-party vendor, Pack remarked, adding that cyberattacks have accelerated to "machine speed" as criminals increasingly use artificial intelligence to probe for vulnerabilities.

"You have this cat and mouse game where cybersecurity experts are trying to patch the vulnerabilities that they find. They're looking for their own vulnerabilities at the same time, they have to play defense against the criminals who are out there trying to steal information or do harm to our systems. I think we're just seeing now this speed of these intrusions ramp up a lot," Pack noted.

TECH OUTAGE CASCADE EXPOSES US VULNERABILITIES TO FOREIGN CYBER THREATS.

In a recent development, A cyber intrusion into the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) could endanger police officers during traffic stops, a retired agent says. (Getty Images, File).

The intrusion follows a September cyberattack in which the extortion group ShinyHunters breached an FBI job portal website and claimed to steal personal records belonging to bureau employees.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

The latest incident also comes as a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found 17 of 22 government agencies were not in compliance with federal cybersecurity regulations.

The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the NCIC breach.

Fox News Digital's James Cirrone and Greg Norman-Diamond, and Fox News' David Spunt contributed to this report.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

Tech Report: The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America.
  • In a recent development, in the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent.
  • Although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America. This essay is adapted from his forthcoming book South Korea’s Grand Strategy: Narratives and the Rise of a Global Nation.

What South Korea Gets Right About Geopolitics.

In a recent development, in the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent. In his remarks, Carney stressed that although the old U.S.-led alliance system was collapsing, middle powers—states that do not have the ability to reshape global politics but that still possess substantial might—were well positioned to pick up the slack. But to do so, Carney argued, they would need to build up their “strength at home” and “act together” to harness their collective power, even in the absence of backing from the world’s hegemon.

Although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious. They noted, correctly, that it would be very difficult for middle powers to build a grand alliance composed of countries as diverse as Brazil, Canada, South Africa, and Turkey. “The path to unity among middle powers is fraught because this group includes rich and poor countries, as well as small and large ones,” wrote the economist Eswar Prasad in February. Carney, however, is right that middle powers have an opportunity to thrive going forward. Even when aligning with great powers, these countries can still exercise greater autonomy by developing national capacity and diversifying external partnerships.

Sources indicate that south Korea offers a prime example of this flexible approach. For decades, Seoul has pursued a middle-power strategy centered on building domestic strength and forging partnerships with democracies everywhere while deepening its alliance with Washington. South Korea has been adaptable, recalibrating its security alignments, economic strategies, and diplomatic roles as regional and global conditions require. This has enabled a country smaller in size than most of the world’s states to punch far above its weight, exercising substantial influence in Asia and beyond.

Not every government can follow Seoul’s path, and South Korea’s strategy has its limits. As Seoul itself acknowledges, middle powers cannot escape great-power competition. But the country has begun to show what middle powers can accomplish when they leverage their partnerships and their own strength to protect their interests and deter larger threats. And by maintaining and even building its ties to the United States while asserting greater autonomy, South Korea has proven that middle powers can strengthen themselves without building whole newly introduced networks—contrary to Carney’s suggestion.

According to recent reports, according to classic international relations theory, grand strategy is the exclusive provenance of great powers. The United States’s effort to contain the Soviet Union during the Cold War is a paradigmatic example; China’s pursuit of global economic primacy is another. Middle powers, by contrast, have little say in such strategies. Instead, these countries are seen as primarily reactive in their foreign policies, navigating around the decisions of the great powers rather than setting the agenda themselves.

But recent history suggests that the division between great and middle powers is less clear-cut than has been assumed. In practice, middle powers very much have their own affirmative visions that they pursue in the world. They have the leeway to decide which threats matter most to them, which partnerships to prioritize, and where to invest scarce resources. Japan, concerned with the threat posed by China, has been quietly exercising leadership in the Indo-Pacific by improving its ties with neighbors, increasing investment and aid to the region, and strengthening its own defense capabilities—all while remaining closely allied with the United States. India, worried about China, Pakistan, and growing economic headwinds, has successfully bolstered partnerships with the United States and other democracies but maintained its relationship with Russia.

Industry observers note that much like Japan and India, South Korea is worried about its neighbors. But for Seoul, this is nothing new. South Korean leaders have been concerned with the very thing Carney fretted about in his Davos speech—becoming collateral damage in conflicts between great powers— since at least the late nineteenth century, when it was caught between China, Japan, and Russia. The country has a well-known proverb, “When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken,” that captures the sentiment that great-power feuds can harm countries caught in the middle.

It has been revealed that to safeguard against this threat, Seoul has long sought to increase its self-reliance through industrial policy. The country transited from light to heavy export industries in the 1970s, turning it into a major player in the chemical, steel, and shipbuilding sectors. State investments helped it become a major global producer of batteries and semiconductors in the present era. South Korea takes great pride in what historians call “the miracle on the Han”—or the country's rapid rise from a war-torn and impoverished state to a rich one during the late twentieth century. They now use the state’s wealth to promote public goods globally, contributing to international development, global health, climate policy, and multilateral bodies.

Sources indicate that seoul has also built up a formidable military, one that experts consistently rank as among the strongest in the world. Today, many South Korean analysts argue that Seoul needs a nuclear arsenal for self-defense, even though the country officially remains under Washington’s nuclear umbrella. The state has simultaneously used its armed prowess to deepen relations with U.S. allies. Seoul, for example, has inked multibillion-dollar arms deals with European buyers, making it a key partner in rebuilding NATO’s industrial capacity. In 2025, it was the second largest supplier of weapons to European NATO members (after the United States). South Korea has also forged defense partnerships in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, widening Seoul's options and reducing its dependence on any single market. South Korea, in other words, has been able to convert its economic resources and bureaucratic capabilities into greater influence by expanding its partnerships, strengthening its voice in international bodies, and helping shape global rules and norms.

Sources indicate that but even as it charts its own path, Seoul has no prepares to abandon the United States, at least in the near future. In fact, the sanctity of the U.S.-South Korean relationship is a significant historical Korean narrative. Many South Koreans see the alliance as a bond inked in blood, thanks to the sacrifice both countries made during the Korean War, when they worked to stop North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, from overrunning the south. Most South Koreans correctly believe that the continued U.S. military presence in the country—currently, 28,500 American troops are stationed on the peninsula—has played a major part in deterring North Korean aggression over the past seven decades.

Industry observers note that at first glance, South Korea’s strategy may seem contradictory. On the one hand, the country wants to deepen its cooperation with the United States, on which it still depends for security. But on the other, it seeks greater autonomy.

Yet these twin goals are not actually at odds. By cultivating ties with Washington, Seoul has gained access to advanced military capabilities and technologies as well as a larger diplomatic platform to expand its regional and global interests. It is in part because of this relationship, for example, that South Korea has had such success at selling weapons to multiple NATO members, including Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Norway, Poland, and Romania. (Seoul has also built up a formidable diplomatic apparatus in its own right.) At the same time, South Korea helps make this compact worthwhile for the United States by providing it with valuable technology, including semiconductor chips. Seoul has also partnered with the Washington to help revive the American shipbuilding industry, agreeing to invest $150 billion in the U.S. sector.

According to recent reports, still, South Korea’s growing push for more independence in its foreign policy does result in some tensions with the United States that cannot easily be resolved. For instance, the current government’s push to give Seoul, not Washington, operational control over both states’ forces on the peninsula in the event of war has been rebuffed by the U.S. military. American commanders instead favor a conditions-based transfer after South Korea has proven it has the capabilities to lead a joint defense, rather than setting a fixed date. The two sides also have not reached a consensus on what role South Korea would play if Taiwan is attacked or blockaded by China.

Yet so far, Seoul has done an effective job at managing these differences. For example, in his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Washington’s allies, including South Korea, of leeching off the United States and not paying their fair share. To extract more from Washington’s partners, Trump has implemented punishing tariffs. In response, South Korea could have been defiant and slapped on retaliatory restrictions, as other U.S. allies did. Instead, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung avoided rebuking the president and worked to meet American demands in ways that heightened the two states’ mutual dependence. For instance, Lee pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States to advance American economic and national security interests, including by purchasing more U.S. military equipment, and to increase South Korean economic support for locally stationed American forces.

According to recent reports, seoul’s strategy has not been a uniform success. The South Korean economy remains exposed to American and Chinese pressure despite its growth and diversification. North Korea is expanding its nuclear and missile forces and deepening military ties with Russia, creating latest security headaches for which Seoul still needs U.S. assistance. The country is politically polarized, resulting in sharp policy shifts that can undermine long-term strategic planning. It also suffers from the lowest birthrate of any country in the world, threatening its tax base and the size of its armed forces. Beyond that, South Korea may not provide the ideal template for every middle power. Not every country in this category has similar economic resources, networks, or ties to the United States.

But on the whole, South Korea’s grand strategy has been effective, and it thus carries broader lessons. For one, it shows how adaptive middle powers can draw on their respective national narratives to find their strengths and to chart a path forward. Perhaps more important, it is proof positive that middle powers can exercise influence and achieve a measure of autonomy even without working together to build a neutral third pole, as Carney urged. It also illustrates that middle powers can remain firmly allied with the United States while developing their own independent capabilities. South Korea, then, demonstrates that states can reduce their vulnerability and widen their political options.

An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the South Korean government was known to be considering developing nuclear weapons.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In June 2026, Google and Voltus unveiled a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
  • Sources indicate that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
  • Utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

In June 2026, Google and Voltus unveiled a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

Sources indicate that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

Utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

Sources indicate that beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

Sources indicate that while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

Industry observers note that wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

It has been revealed that bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

Industry observers note that the appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wright and Turner examine growing concerns over the federal government's cybersecurity preparedness, potential vulnerabilities across government agencies and the risks posed by increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

A sweeping federal watchdog report found that 17 of 22 major civilian agencies failed to fully address key cybersecurity planning guidance, warning that the shortcomings could leave government systems more vulnerable to cyberattacks and operational disruptions.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) released its findings this week, identifying gaps at the Departments of Homeland Security (DHS), Justice (DOJ), State, Treasury and Health and Human Services (HHS), among others.

The report examined whether agencies had incorporated selected federal guidance into their plans for implementing zero trust architecture, a cybersecurity approach requiring users, devices and systems to be verified before accessing protected networks.

RETIRED FBI AGENT WARNS NCIC BREACH COULD THREATEN POLICE SAFETY DURING TRAFFIC STOPS.

Recent findings suggest that the GAO report discovered that 17 of 22 federal agencies did not meet cybersecurity planning standards. (Getty Images).

Only five of the 22 agencies fully addressed the selected guidance as of August 2026, prompting GAO to concern 40 recommendations to the remaining 17.

"Agencies would therefore be at increased risk of cyberattacks that could interrupt operations or otherwise compromise agency resources," GAO warned.

HHS received six recommendations, the most of any agency reviewed, after investigators found that it lacked a documented enterprise-wide zero trust implementation plan covering all its information systems.

Although individual divisions were pursuing cybersecurity improvements, GAO warned that the absence of a unified strategy could prevent department leadership from maintaining a coherent view of its security modernization efforts.

HHS agreed with the recommendations and noted it planned to develop an actionable department-wide strategy by the second quarter of fiscal year 2027.

CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES.

The Department of Commerce received four recommendations after investigators identified shortcomings in its cybersecurity planning documentation.

Commerce officials told GAO that staffing losses had significantly constrained the department's zero trust working group, limiting its ability to coordinate improvements and maintain comprehensive documentation.

Industry observers note that at DHS, investigators found that the department had not fully documented cybersecurity maturity levels across all its high-value assets and high-impact systems. Officials attributed the incomplete assessments partly to lengthy government shutdowns during the preceding fiscal year.

DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS.

Sources indicate that GAO attributed many of the incomplete reports to the prior fiscal year's government shutdown. (iStock).

DOJ similarly cited resource constraints for incomplete assessments of critical systems, while State and Treasury were among the agencies that had only partially documented cybersecurity maturity levels.

GAO warned that incomplete assessments could leave agency leadership without the visibility necessary to determine where additional cybersecurity resources are needed.

Investigators also found that 11 agencies had only partially documented procedures for identifying actors within their IT environments, including certain non-person entities such as software applications and service accounts.

The watchdog warned that incomplete identification procedures could hinder efforts to ensure only authorized owners and systems access government resources.

TRUMP’S NATIONAL CYBER DIRECTOR SEAN CAIRNCROSS FIRED AMID WIDESPREAD TECH OUTAGES.

The report found that 11 agencies had only partially documented cybersecurity procedures. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images).

The findings come years after the Biden administration directed federal agencies to adopt zero trust cybersecurity principles through a 2021 executive order, followed by additional guidance in 2022 and 2024. Despite those directives, GAO found that 17 of 22 agencies still had not fully addressed selected cybersecurity planning requirements and guidance as of August 2026.

Thirteen agencies agreed with GAO's 40 recommendations, while four neither agreed nor disagreed. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission, one of the four, provided documentation demonstrating that it had already addressed both recommendations, which GAO verified.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and all 17 agencies identified in the report for comment.

"Absent a full implementation of ZTA requirements and guidance, agencies will lack an appropriate roadmap to fully incorporate and maintain an effective zero trust architecture," GAO concluded.

#122444. Pop Culture Still Can’t Figure Out Drone Warfare

Pop Culture Still Can’t Figure Out Drone Warfare

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore.
  • Industry observers note that hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo.
  • Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In a recent development, military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

Industry observers note that hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light shows. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

Military experts don’t really talk much about a “front line” in the war in Ukraine anymore. They prefer the term “kill zone,” used to describe the 10- to 20-mile-wide no-man’s-land between the two armies. The reason for this conceptual shift is simple: Omnipresent drone surveillance has made it nearly impossible for anyone to get close to enemy-controlled territory without being detected.

Hollywood doesn’t seem to have gotten the memo. In a recent episode of the hit TV show Lioness, Zoe Saldaña’s character leads a small group of U.S. covert operators on a secret mission to capture an enemy spy who is hanging out with Russian forces in Ukraine. To do so, the Americans have to cross from the Ukrainian side to the Russian one—which they do by simply walking across, in broad daylight, tightly bunched together. In the real world, they would have been shredded by kamikaze drones or artillery as soon as they started their stroll. Plus, the sky above them is filled with so many drones that it calls to mind one of those spectacular drone light shows. But that’s far from the modus operandi in Ukraine: You don’t need mega-swarms to keep a large area under surveillance; a bunch of individual operators searching in assigned sectors is enough. Compounding the absurdity, Saldaña’s character and her team only get attacked on their way back from their mission. Did it really take that long for the Russians to notice them?

Industry observers note that but perhaps the makers of Lioness deserve some credit simply for tackling the subject. Four and a half years after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, cultural depictions of how the war is actually being fought are strikingly thin on the ground. A few journalists have written solid first-person accounts of the conflict, and documentary filmmakers, many of them Ukrainian, have explored it with astonishing intimacy. Yet their works have reached relatively small audiences. Where are the gripping stories for the broader public?

Combat drones have certainly made a mark on the broader culture. You see them everywhere, from movies like The Terminal List: Dark Wolf , where an assassin uses a drone to blow up a car, to the BBC’s police procedural Vigil, which includes a sequence in which military drones are turned against their own side by a hostile hacker. It’s striking how often drones turn up in dystopian science fiction films—such as The Gorge, where two snipers fight off autonomous drones, and The Outer Threat, in which a man with a dramatic secret has to protect his family from a hostile government equipped with drone swarms. A few years ago, the drone designs in these films probably would have resembled the exquisitely engineered aircraft of the so-called global war on terror. Now, even sci-fi creators seem to be favoring small quadcopters like the ones used by Ukrainians in their fight against Russia. But few of these cultural references involve depictions of war.

According to recent reports, retired Australian Army Maj. Gen. Mick Ryan, who has carefully tracked the war in Ukraine, argues that pop culture can be a useful way of helping politicians and the public stay abreast of developments on the battlefield. “Military doctrine is inaccessible to most people, including a lot of people in the military,” he noted. “Whether it’s movies, television, books, or podcasts, [pop culture] can be an excellent way of making complex military and technological intersections accessible to a broader range of people.” Ryan practices what he preaches: He’s written an excellent speculative novel, White Sun War, about a hypothetical conflict over Taiwan, which includes detailed scenes of Chinese and U.S. forces fighting with the help of autonomous unmanned ground vehicles. Ryan’s fictional technology is ahead of what the Russians and Ukrainians have developed in their war—but only slightly.

A Ukrainian soldier fires at a drone flying overhead in Kramatorsk, Ukraine, on Nov. 11. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images.

Could it be that drone warfare is just too complicated for compelling storytelling? By now, both sides in the Russia-Ukraine war have deployed a wide variety of drones on land, at sea, and in the air. None of these machines exists in isolation. They’re part of complex battlefield ecosystems that encompass reconnaissance, strike, and (increasingly) supply. Lately the Ukrainians have even been using ground drones to evacuate wounded soldiers. The intensity of the conflict has driven an astonishing pace of innovation, often involving the intricacies of maintaining reliable communications and targeting in environments saturated with electronic warfare measures. Responses have included drones controlled by fiber-optic cables (which can’t be jammed, unlike radio signals) and increasing reliance on artificial intelligence systems that can keep drones on target even when their links with operators go down.

According to recent reports, perhaps it’s no surprise that outsiders have a hard time keeping up. In October, video game publisher Activision released Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest installment of its long-running franchise. (A reminder: The global gaming industry is way bigger than the movie industry.) The story revolves around an imagined North Korean invasion of South Korea, and its depiction of the intense combat that such a conflict would entail is amazingly convincing. The game’s creators have put a huge amount of effort into getting the details right (even extending to hiring a dialect coach to consult on the different forms of Korean spoken by the characters).

Seeing the effort the game’s designers put into verisimilitude, it’s all the more surprising that drones have a very limited role. This omission is especially odd given that North Korea has dispatched large numbers of troops to help Russia in the war against Ukraine—in part so that Kim Jong Un’s forces could learn about the intricacies of drone warfare. The game’s creators seem to have been oblivious to this. When a joint South Korean-U.S. force counters the invasion with an amphibious counterattack, the intensity of the combat recalls the opening scenes of Saving Private Ryan. Yet neither side in the fight deploys drones on land or in the sky—although this is exactly the sort of combat in which modern militaries are already working frantically to incorporate the lessons of Ukraine.

In 1983, two movies sought to educate and alarm the public about the risks of new technologies.

From the president on down, many Americans still do not grasp the implications of drones and other threats.

Industry observers note that part of the problem is surely that the remote-controlled, seemingly anonymous nature of modern drones diminishes their narrative potential. Real-life drone operations often involve long and meticulous searches and extended loitering—not exactly the stuff of high drama. Those brutal Ukrainian drone attack videos that now populate social media show only the climactic moments that follow hours and hours of painstaking preparation and reconnaissance. This could be why we see some video game designers creating drones with machine guns on them; in real life, that’s a generally useless approach, since the recoil from the guns would destabilize the drone, perhaps fatally. But shooting feels a lot more satisfying than hitting a distant target that you can only see on a screen.

That video games present such a distorted vision of contemporary war is especially ironic considering that the gaming industry has significantly shaped drone warfare. Military drone controllers are often modeled on the ones used by gamers, which hugely simplifies training.

Sources indicate that ukrainian filmmakers have found themselves confronting similar narrative challenges. The fascinating upcoming movie Killhouse, which was shot in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military, features plenty of scenes that convey a vivid sense of the peculiarities of drone warfare. The film turns on the fate of a civilian couple who are lured into the gray zone between the front lines by Russian gangsters who are holding their daughter for ransom. Unlike the blissful U.S. soldiers in Lioness, the desperate mother and father are immediately detected by both the Russians and Ukrainians as soon as they enter the area. The Russians swiftly shell them, while the Ukrainians devise a complicated, drone-assisted strategy for their rescue—and, ultimately, the daughter’s. One particularly nail-biting sequence depicts an operator trying to use a drone to guide a character through a minefield, even though he has no clear way of communicating with her.

Industry observers note that the movie’s creators would have done well to stop there, after showing us real-life drones in real-life situations. Unfortunately, even they apparently felt the need to juice up their story by introducing a set of as-yet-non-existent drones that use facial recognition systems for their targets. (That capability is pretty useful for the Chinese surveillance state; why you would need it on a battlefield without expansive access to a database of enemy faces remains unclear.) At the moment of a critical showdown, these ultra-high-tech drones are used simply as brute force to knock out several Russian soldiers—all that fancy equipment ends up effectively serving the same purpose as a couple of big rocks.

Industry observers note that perhaps the shortcomings of movies and video games aren’t worth taking so seriously. There’s no requirement for ultra-realism, and no one should exaggerate the extent to which popular culture drives the decisions of policymakers. But is it just a coincidence that Western militaries, policymakers, and politicians are still failing to learn from the war in Ukraine after all these years?

A still from Killhouse. Ukrainian Film Division.

U.S. and other Western military bases are still plagued by drone incursions of unknown provenance; the one thing that’s clear is that many of these drones, which are equipped to resist powerful jamming, aren’t operated by hobbyists. In recent weeks, the U.S. Air Force has cited the threat of drone attacks in connection with at least two major alerts at air bases in Britain. Decision-makers were apparently reacting to fears that Iran might launch an attack emulating Kyiv’s stunning Operation Spiderweb, when Ukraine managed to destroy a number of Russian strategic bombers by launching drones that were smuggled into Russia on freight trucks. European NATO members have experienced various drone incursions, as well as confronting actual attacks. Even the Australians have had to deal with mysterious drone sightings near their bases. The technology is proliferating; the problem can no longer be written off.

Industry observers note that we’re still waiting for the Hollywood blockbuster that brings home the impact of drone warfare to ordinary voters—something like the 1927 film Wings, one of the first to familiarize a broad audience with the significance of military aircraft. But the lack of popular familiarity with the changed nature of war is no excuse for the complacency of Western leaders.

Industry observers note that christian Caryl is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a former Moscow bureau chief for Newsweek and U.S. News & World Report, and the author of Strange Rebels: 1979 and the Birth of the 21st Century. X: @ccaryl.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • After more than two decades in office and weeks of ballot counting, North Carolina Republican Virginia Foxx, chair of the powerful House Rules Committee, has conceded defeat in her reelection bid.
  • Retired journalist Chuck Hubbard bested Foxx in a nail-biter of a race — he was up by about 0.1 percentage point, or 330 votes out of nearly 300,000 ballots cast when the Associated Press called the race on Sunday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., presides over a House Rules Committee hearing in the Capitol on July 20. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After more than two decades in office and weeks of ballot counting, North Carolina Republican Virginia Foxx, chair of the powerful House Rules Committee, has conceded defeat in her reelection bid.

Retired journalist Chuck Hubbard bested Foxx in a nail-biter of a race — he was up by about 0.1 percentage point, or 330 votes out of nearly 300,000 ballots cast when the Associated Press called the race on Sunday.

Foxx lost in a rematch against Hubbard, whom she beat by almost 20 points in their 2024 race.

It has been revealed that “Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process,” Hubbard wrote in a Facebook post Sunday. “Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.”.

Foxx was swept from office as part of a midterm surge that will put Democrats in charge of the House with the largest majority for either party since 1993 at 258 seats and counting; two other races where the Democrat is right now leading have yet to be called.

A 260-seat majority would be the largest since 1989, according to the House historian's office.

Until recently, Foxx's district was solidly Republican and had not elected a Democrat since 1992.

It took nearly three weeks for the race to be called as provisional and mail-in ballots were added to the total. Three days after the election, as the final votes were tallied, Foxx requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers to monitor the counting process.

Recent findings suggest that “Election integrity is not a mere suggestion — it is the keystone of free and fair elections that have always guided the course of our nation throughout history,” she wrote in a Facebook post at the time. “The counting process for the 5th District election has not halted. The count is ongoing in accordance with North Carolina state law.”.

On November 16, with the race still officially uncalled, Foxx requested a full recount; however the recount confirmed that Hubbard had won.

“After a hard-fought and thorough election process, the voters of the Fifth Congressional District exercised their constitutional rights and made their voices heard,” Foxx noted in a statement Sunday. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina.”.

As the recount was underway, Foxx filed for reelection in 2028, at which point she will be 85 years old.

In her 11 terms in the House, Foxx built a reputation as a sharp-witted social conservative, unafraid to offer unfiltered views. She has also been a key ally of President Donald Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

It has been revealed that foxx is the first Republican woman to serve as chair of the Rules Committee. The late Rep. Louise M. Slaughter, D-N.Y., who led the panel from 2007 to 2011, was the only other woman to hold the gavel.

On the Rules panel, Foxx has been a workhorse for House Republicans’ agenda, often working late into the night and amending rules text on the fly in response to the high-stakes intraparty negotiations that have dominated Johnson’s speakership.

Foxx’s acerbic wit is well matched on Rules by the panel’s ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. The two often spar over policy and procedure alike.

According to recent reports, foxx is the only woman chairing a House committee in the 119th Congress. According to the House historian's office, the last time the House had no female committee chairs was from 2005 to 2007, during the 109th Congress.

Next in line in seniority to become the top Rules Republican is Minnesota Rep. Michelle Fischbach, who's expressed interest previously and got some practice sitting in for Foxx during committee hearings and managing rules on the floor when Foxx was away.

Before her Rules role, Foxx was the top Republican on the House Education and Workforce panel from 2017 to the end of 2024.

She has been a vocal supporter of conservative efforts to abolish the Education Department and noted she would do so “in a heartbeat." She points to the 10th Amendment, which says that the powers not delegated in the Constitution to the federal government are reserved for the states and individuals. Education, she asserts, is therefore not a federal responsibility.

As a former school board member for 12 years, she notes that the government telling school boards how to work is “not the way this country should be operating.”.

According to recent reports, A devout Catholic, Foxx is well known on Capitol Hill for her religious faith, attending weekly prayer meetings and Bible study sessions. She starts each day “with a prayer for wisdom and strength to do God’s will,” she told CQ Roll Call.

In 2016, she published “God is in the House: Congressional Testimonies of Faith,” a book of essays on faith and legislative work by members of Congress.

In a recent development, the Rules Committee has experienced relatively high turnover in recent years. Foxx’s predecessor, former-Rep. Michael Burgess, R-Texas, succeeded Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., in April 2024 after Cole departed to chair the Appropriations Committee. Cole himself only held the position for just over a year after taking over for McGovern, though he became the panel's top Republican in 2019.

She served in the state Senate from 1995 to 2004, and when Republican Richard M. Burr left his House seat to run for the Senate in 2004 Foxx entered the race to succeed him. She prevailed over seven other Republicans in the primary and went on to defeat her Democratic challenger in November. At 61, she was one of the oldest members of the freshman class of 2005.

North Carolina’s 5th District encompasses much of northwestern North Carolina, including the Blue Ridge Mountains and the foothills of the Piedmont.

The Paradox of American Credibility

📖 0% read
